transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-05-04
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Elena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Cascade CTO), Liam Chen (ML Engineer), Sana Malik (Security), Omar Qureshi (Data Eng)

Summary (auto): high level model selection, context window and multilingual requirements, next steps to run benchmarks and share security docs.

00:00 Elena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Elena from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Marco from our engineering team. How's everyone doing?
00:06 Priya: Good — thanks. Little hectic but we're ready.
00:10 Elena: Great. Quick agenda: understand your use cases, what you're optimizing for (latency, cost, accuracy), constraints (data residency, SSO), and then go over model options and next steps.
00:20 Priya: Sounds good. At a high level we're building a multimodal docs assistant for our enterprise customers. Big requirements: 1) end-to-end retrieval + generation over very long documents — think 50k to 150k token contexts, 2) multilingual — English, Spanish, French, Japanese at minimum, 3) ability to call internal tools/APIs from the model (tool-calling), 4) strict security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs, and EU data residency for a subset of customers.
00:42 Marco: Got it. For the context length, are you doing retrieval-first (RAG) with chunking or are you expecting full longer-context models to run natively?
00:49 Liam: Right now retrieval + chunked RAG but we're investigating longer-context models to avoid complex chunking logic. We want to know tradeoffs — whether to run a 100k+ context open model vs using 32k + good retrieval and cache.
01:05 Marco: Yeah, so tradeoffs: long-context models are more expensive per token and may have lower throughput on some hardware, but they simplify pipeline. With Redwood Dedicated you can pin larger-context model variants and get reserved throughput; Hosted can work but we'd discuss SLOs and burst. Also caching/prefix KV cache can reduce cost if many queries hit similar prefixes — though nlp transcriptions sometimes call it KV cash in notes, heh.
01:28 Priya: (laughs) we've seen 'KV cash' too.
01:30 Elena: On multilingual: open models differ a lot. Mistral-style and Llama-derivatives often have decent English but vary on low-resource languages. For Spanish/French most recent open models are fine; Japanese is hit or miss depending on tokenization. We can share a model comparison matrix.
01:48 Marco: To add — quantization can impact multilingual quality; 4-bit quant performs okay on English but some languages degrade. We'll run our benchmark with multilingual samples to measure quality delta.
02:00 Sana: From security side, key questions: can we run on Private deployment (VPC / on-prem) with our own KMS/HSM? We have strict regulatory customers in EU so data residency matters.
02:12 Marco: Yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS and on-prem install. Dedicated also offers region pinning and isolated GPU pools if you want Redwood-managed infra with guaranteed throughput. Hosted API is simplest but for strict EU residency and our KMS requirements we typically recommend Dedicated or Private.
02:30 Priya: Ok. On tool-calling: we need function calling to retrieve structured data from internal APIs and to trigger actions. Does Redwood support that across Hosted and Private? Any limitations for open models?
02:42 Elena: Yes, we expose a function/tool calling interface. For hosted we have built-in integrations and can proxy calls; for Private you can wire up your internal tool endpoints directly. Note: some open model flavors have native structured output ability, others require prompt engineering or a small wrapper model to enforce strict schema.
03:05 Liam: Are there recommended models for tool-calling + structured output? We've seen Anthropic and OpenAI examples but we're trying to stay with open models.
03:13 Marco: For open models, the best bets for structured output are models with instruction-tuning and strong RLHF-like alignment. Mistral-based and Llama-derivs with instruction finetunes work well; also some community-tuned models have good JSON stability. We'll include examples in the comparison.
03:30 Priya: Performance SLOs — we need p95 latency under 750ms for short queries (<=1k tokens) and throughput for batch summarization jobs overnight. How do hosted vs dedicated affect that?
03:42 Marco: Hosted has shared pools, so latency can vary; we have latency SLOs for paid tiers but Dedicated gives predictable P95 and reserved slots for concurrency. For heavy batch jobs, Dedicated or Private with autoscale policies will be cheaper and more controllable.
03:55 Priya: Price is also a factor — cost per 1k tokens and reserved capacity pricing.
04:01 Elena: We'll include both per-token price estimates and reserved capacity numbers. Also Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization/batching to lower unit cost — we'll run that as part of POC.
04:14 Omar: For benchmarking, we'd like to run small perf tests on our data. Can Redwood run a POC where we test two open models on hosted first and then move to dedicated?
04:23 Marco: Absolutely. Typical approach: run initial quality and perf tests on Hosted to validate models and prompt patterns, then spin up Dedicated for production-level throughput. For Private we can do an on-prem pilot once infra requirements are defined.
04:36 Priya: Any docs on model artifacts and kernel selection? We have specialized sequences and some models are sensitive to seq len.
04:44 Marco: We do model profiles that show kernel selection, supported max context, quantization compatibility, and recommended hardware. We'll share the model catalog link and a sample profile for a 64k-context variant.
04:56 Liam: A few gotchas: tokenizer differences change token counts; also embeddings and reranking models matter for RAG.
05:04 Elena: Right. We'll include a suggested stack: 1) retrieval + embedding index, 2) reranker, 3) a model for generation (long-context or 32k + prompt engineering), 4) caching. For embeddings we can recommend specific open models for multilingual similarity.
05:20 Sana: Audit logs and RBAC — how granular are the logs and can we push them to our SIEM?
05:27 Marco: Yes, audit logs and trace hooks can forward to your SIEM; we support SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC in Dedicated/Private. Hosted supports audit logs for enterprise tiers.
05:41 Priya: Ok. Let's talk about concrete model candidates. Which open models should we benchmark first for our use case?
05:49 Marco: Candidate list to start: Mistral-instruct variants (good instruction-following), LLamaX-like 70b tuned models (if you need high quality), Long-context variants (64k / 128k) like LongForm models (community variants), and lighter 13-30b models with aggressive quant for cost-sensitive use cases. We'll put them in a matrix with quality, latency, cost, and multilingual scores.
06:12 Liam: For long context, is 100k viable in hosted?
06:16 Marco: Technically yes for some model variants, but cost and latency go up and throughput drops. Hosted can support it but you'd likely want Dedicated to meet strict p95 SLOs. Also watch out for KV cache evictions — long contexts mean larger KV caches and memory needs.
06:32 Priya: What about tool calling latency — we will need sub-second responses when tool call occurs. If a model triggers a function that calls our internal API, latency will include network hop. Any best practices?
06:44 Marco: Best practice: do a fast validation step in-model to decide whether to call a tool, then call asynchronously and stream partial responses back. Also colocate services where possible (region pinning) and use Dedicated to reduce network jitter.
06:58 Elena: We'll include an example architecture diagram in the follow-up docs (shared link).
07:02 Priya: Great. For privacy/regulatory customers, how do you handle logging of prompts/PII?
07:09 Marco: You can configure redaction and opt-out of prompt logging on Private/Dedicated. Hosted enterprise tier offers configurable retention and encryption-at-rest with customer-managed keys. We'll share the retention policy doc.
07:24 Sana: We need to review SOC2 and the encryption controls — please share the doc and maybe a checklist.
07:30 Elena: Will do. We'll attach SOC2, network diagram, and a KMS options brief.
07:34 Priya: About evaluation metrics: besides BLEU-like scores, we care about hallucination rate on Q&A, correctness for tool-calling, and multilingual F1 for extraction.
07:44 Marco: We'll define prompt templates and evaluation harness; suggest sample metrics and a small labeled set you can provide for the POC.
07:53 Liam: Timeline — we're aiming for a POC within 3-4 weeks, then a pilot end of Q3. Is that realistic?
08:00 Elena: Yes, that's reasonable. Typical timeline: week 0-1 discovery + baseline models, week 1-2 hosted perf/quality tests, week 2-4 Dedicated pilot if needed. We'll align resources.
08:12 Priya: Anything else?
08:14 Omar: Can you share the benchmark sheet link now?
08:17 Marco: Sure — shared benchmark sheet here: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/CRM-48291 (mock link). We'll populate it with candidate models and test cases.
08:28 Priya: Perfect. Ok recap and next steps please.
08:32 Elena: Recap: 1) Redwood will send model comparison matrix + pricing and SOC2/network/KMS docs; 2) Marco will provision benchmark template and run initial hosted tests with 3 candidate models including a long-context variant and a quantized 30b variant; 3) Cascade will provide multilingual sample dataset and latency SLOs; 4) schedule technical deep dive (Marco + Liam) next Wed.
08:54 Priya: Good. We'll review and confirm.
09:00 Elena: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email and post the docs in the benchmark sheet.
09:05 Meeting end.

Notes on transcription quality: some mis-spellings (KV cash), occasional speaker attribution as 'Marco' vs 'Speaker 2' in raw export, filler words preserved.

Shared artifacts: model comparison template (link in next steps), SOC2 report (link to be sent), benchmark sheet: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/CRM-48291
